A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same bijection-learning work. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, and complete appendices support comparison, including material moved between sections and appendices.

before.justification: V1 reports original jailbreak evaluations, parameter sweeps, MMLU measurements, failure-mode analyses, and a guarded-system experiment.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and reports additional baseline comparisons, model-family scaling evaluations, and guarded-system experiments.

M1.justification: The encoding, in-context teaching, decoding, denoising, and best-of-n procedure remain unchanged. Dispersion reparameterizes fixed size as d = 26 - F; encoding length was already varied in v1. Appendices A and B retain the same templates and classifier instructions.

E1.justification: AdvBench-50, HarmBench, HarmBench-35, and MMLU remain. V2 Section 5 adds a custom set of 100 benign intents to evaluate guardrail false rejections, a focused extension beyond the existing harmful-input and capability evaluations.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated PAIR, TAP, GCG-transfer, and an 11-encoding ensemble against the main benchmark results; v1 Table 1 contained only bijection learning. The universal-attack comparison also changes: v1 Figure 4 compares selected encodings with Pliny, whereas v2 Appendix F compares the retained selected encodings with average-case bijections.

E3.justification: V2 adds comparison protocols, including matched PAIR query budgets, a 58-query TAP budget, and GCG transfer from Llama Guard 3. Scaling evaluations add Claude 3 Sonnet, Llama 3.1, and Gemini 1.5 configurations. Guard testing expands to three guard models with common encodings and separate harmful/benign budgets. The reported human-judging rubric expands to PREFS with a copyright exception; this does not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: V1 Appendix C's single-guard experiment becomes a substantially expanded capability-parity and overrefusal analysis in v2 Section 5. Figure 7 extends scaling analysis across four model families. Conversely, v2 narrows the failure-mode plots to digit attacks on HarmBench-35 and no longer separately reports the 20-teaching-example MMLU conditions shown in v1 Figure 6.

E5.justification: Both versions display error bars for MMLU attack conditions. However, v1 Figure 6 also shows separate baseline estimates with error bars; v2 Figures 6 and 11 replace these with horizontal baseline lines without displayed uncertainty. Neither version specifies seed counts or the error-bar construction.

E6.justification: The proposed method's Table 1 scores remain unchanged, including 86.3% for Claude 3.5 Sonnet on HarmBench. V2 adds extensive comparator results: the corresponding ensemble, PAIR, TAP, and GCG-transfer scores are 20.9%, 9.7%, 10.3%, and 0.3%. It also adds model-family findings and expanded guard results, while removing Pliny scores. Revised guard results should not be interpreted as same-setting performance changes from v1's explicitly LLM-only evaluation.

T1.justification: The ASR definition is retained, and dispersion is an equivalent reparameterization of fixed size. Encoding length already existed in v1's experiments. Neither version supplies formal theorems or proofs; the expanded scaling and computational-overload discussion remains empirical and interpretive.

C1.justification: The central claims of effective, practically endless attacks that exploit increasing model capabilities remain. V2 refines the headline contribution around universal, scale-adaptive sampling and explicitly presents the Pareto-frontier/computational-overload account as a contribution in Section 1.3, extending the earlier emphasis on scaling laws and failure modes.

C2.justification: V1 Section 5 anticipates that a sufficiently capable output filter could detect encoded harmful content. V2 Section 5 finds only modest mitigation even with a capability-matched guard, while attributing Haiku's apparent protection to severe overrefusal. V2 also develops computational overload as an alternative to mismatched generalization and identifies Gemini as an exception to the two-regime scaling pattern. The standalone limitations text remains unchanged.

D1.justification: V2 adds baseline implementation settings, identifies GPT-4o-2024-08-06, and labels Figure 7's MMLU evaluation as a 100-question subset. It removes v1's explicit 2048-token response limit. The detailed prompt and classifier appendices are unchanged. These are documentation changes, not evidence that previously unspecified settings changed.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion shifts from broad safety, attacks, and robustness coverage to optimization-, persuasion-, and encoding-based attacks, with substantial distinctions concerning access, universality, and adaptability. V2 adds positioning against prompt-fuzzing approaches and mismatched-generalization explanations, supported by new citations including GPTFuzzer, Hayase et al., and Kotha et al.; much of the earlier defense-oriented discussion is removed.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methods exposition, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Desiderata move into the introduction, experiments gain a dedicated baseline section, guard evaluation moves into the main text, and universal-attack results move to Appendix F. Terminology changes throughout from fixed size and scale-agnostic to dispersion and scale-adaptive.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview to show the existing denoiser, restructures Table 1 around models and comparator rows, and replaces the combined scaling plot with four family panels. Failure-mode and guard figures are substantially redesigned. MMLU panels are split between the main text and Appendix E, and appendix tables are reorganized. Figures 9 and 10 retain their underlying graphics.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important evidential gaps: Table 1 directly tests competing methods supporting the comparative claim, and Section 5 replaces speculative guard effectiveness with capability-parity and benign-input controls. Expanded scaling analysis also exposes a meaningful Gemini exception. These changes substantially improve validation and qualify the paper's interpretations despite unchanged headline attack scores. Removing the Pliny comparison and some uncertainty and supplementary detail is a drawback, but the stronger comparative evidence and better-controlled defense analysis outweigh those losses.
